title: Hotspot reservation and KV grease layer for dedicated SLAs
creator: Leah Chen
description: Reduce cold-start tail latency and stabilize throughput for Dedicated tenants by reserving a small fast-residency 'hotspot' for high-probability model shards and introducing a lightweight 'grease' layer to bias KV cache population. This ticket implements the allocator, admission rules, and runtime hooks required to: (1) reserve transient residency for tenant hotsets; (2) opportunistically populate a thin hot KV layer during low-util windows; and (3) integrate with autoscaler and SLA checks so reserved capacity does not violate throughput guarantees.
acceptance_criteria: Median cold-start token latency for reserved-tenants decreases by >=60% compared to baseline (measured on synthetic burst profile)
Top-500 tenant hotset KV hit-rate >= 85% within first 30s after burst onset in lab replay tests
No degradation in sustained throughput (qps) for other tenants beyond 3% during grease-layer load windows
Autoscaler respects hotspot reservations: scale-up decisions account for reserved capacity and do not evict hot shards under normal policy
Full rollout through canary fleet with automated rollback on 99th-percentile latency regression > 15%
design_notes: Allocator: small, per-node in-memory reservation table that tracks hot shards by (model, shard-range, tenant, weight-version) and a soft-lease TTL (default 90s).

Grease layer: ephemeral LRU ring (configurable slots) populated with compact KV entries (only keys + short value fingerprints) to speed early cache checks and avoid full weight materialization unless cold-miss persists.
Loader: background chunked streamer that pulls full weights for reserved shards with bandwidth caps and priority classes. Uses backoff when system-wide memory pressure is high.

Admission controller: evaluates incoming burst signals (rps spike, queue length, recent success ratio) and grants hotspot reservations up to a per-tenant cap, with higher priority for reserved Dedicated contracts.
Integration points: autoscaler signals (node-util, queue-pressure), runtime memory monitor, routing policy to prefer nodes with matching hotspot residency for low-latency paths.
Metrics: track reservation_count, grease_hit_rate, grease_evictions, time_to_full_weight_load, reservation_failure_reasons.
rollout_plan: Stage 1 (lab): unit + integration tests with replayed traffic against a dedicated test cluster (2 weeks)
Stage 2 (canary): enable for 5% of dedicated fleet (low-risk tenants) for 1 week, monitor latency/throughput and autoscaler interactions
Stage 3 (tiered rollout): expand to 25% then 60% with 48h observation windows; enable config flags per-tenant so enterprise customers can opt-out
Stage 4 (GA): default-on for Dedicated with tenant-facing docs and console controls (reservation caps, priority level)
Rollback: automatic rollback if 99p latency regresses > 15% or grease_eviction_rate exceeds threshold for 12h
test_plan: Synthetic burst tests: short 30s spikes at 5x steady qps across 1k models to validate hit-rate targets
Long-tail soak: 72-hour run with mixed traffic to validate no memory-pressure-induced OOMs or global throughput regressions
Chaos: node restarts and network partitions to ensure reservations recover and do not leak
Billing/regression: ensure reservation bookkeeping aligns with Dedicated commit accounting and does not double-count capacity
metrics: grease_hit_rate: percent of inference requests served via grease-layer check
time_to_full_weight_load: duration between reservation grant and full weight residency
cold_start_p50/p90/p99: token latency for first requests after model activation
reservation_success_rate: fraction of admission requests granted
background_load_bandwidth: average MB/s used by the stream loader
tradeoffs: Memory vs. tail latency: increasing grease slots improves hit-rate but raises per-node memory pressure and eviction churn
Complexity vs. predictability: richer admission heuristics reduce false positives but make debugging harder for SREs
Fairness: giving Dedicated tenants reservation priority can increase cold-starts for general-purpose tenants during extreme bursts
Billing alignment: reserving capacity impacts unit economics; must coordinate with finance to avoid under- or over-charging
open_questions: What default reservation cap per-tenant balances SLA gains with global memory constraints? (start 10% of node RAM allocated to grease layer?)
Should the grease layer store compressed mini-values or only fingerprints to avoid privacy leakage under multi-tenant scenarios?
How to reconcile reservation accounting with autoscaler prediction windows to avoid oscillation when reservations expire?
Do we need an operator-facing circuit breaker to globally disable all reservations in emergency?
comments: 2025-06-12 Leah Chen: Created ticket after post-mortem on burst incident (INC-2025-06-09) where two large tenants experienced 5-10x cold-start tails.

2025-06-18 Omar Gómez: Spike complete. Prototype allocator + grease-layer proof-of-concept shows 3x improvement in early-hit rates for synthetic hotsets. Recorded memory overhead ~120MB/node for 128-slot grease ring.
2025-06-23 PM review (Ravi Patel): Requested explicit failure modes and cost accounting; added billing and billing-related test steps.
2025-06-26 Design review: agreed to keep grease entries as fingerprints only for first iteration; full-value load behind strict TTL and memory checks.

2025-06-30 QA: started lab replay tests; initial canary config baked into runtime flags. Observed small increase in eviction churn under artificial low-memory test; tuning needed for eviction thresholds.
2025-07-01 SRE (Maria Alvarez): Running cluster soak overnight with canary; monitoring reservation_success_rate and autoscaler interactions. No regressions observed so far.
